title: The Rasch model
text:
What this is for
Sum scores treat every item as interchangeable: a correct answer is worth one point no matter which item it came from. Yet items differ, and the chance of getting any one of them right does not rise in a straight line with the sum score (Where CTT breaks). What is the simplest model that takes items seriously? The Rasch model (Rasch, 1960), with one parameter per person and one per item, on the same scale. That parsimony buys some unusual properties, chief among them that the sum score is all the model needs to know about a person, and it makes demands of the data. This lesson is about both.

title: The Rasch model
The Rasch model
text:
Core ideas

From logistic regression to the Rasch model






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: we regressed 40 chess problems on the players’ Elo ratings, \(\Pr(y = 1) = \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)/(1 + \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x))\). Giving each problem its own intercept raised the Elo slope from 0.50 to 0.83. Problem Y15 stood out: about as hard as Y29, but success on it barely moved with Elo. That lesson ended on a question: what if each player had an unknown parameter of their own instead of an observed Elo rating?



The Rasch model is the answer. It keeps the shape of the logistic regression, but everything on the right-hand side is unknown. For person \(j\) and item \(i\), \[\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \frac{\exp(\theta_j - b_i)}{1 + \exp(\theta_j - b_i)}.\]

\(\theta_j\) is the person’s ability, an idealized version of the sum score. It, and it alone, determines how a person performs on the items. It takes the place of \(\beta_1 \times \text{Elo}\).
\(b_i\) is the item’s difficulty, the item intercept with its sign flipped. When \(\theta = b\), the odds of a correct response are even.

Plotting the probability of a correct response against \(\theta\) for a single item gives the item characteristic curve (ICC). Move the difficulty around and watch what happens.

Try it: an item characteristic curve


Code
viewof icc_b = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Difficulty b"})
viewof icc_a = Inputs.range([0.2, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a (Rasch: a = 1)"})
viewof icc_norm = Inputs.toggle({label: "Overlay the normal CDF", value: false})

























Code
icc_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, icc_b, icc_a), curve: "This item"},
  ...(icc_norm ? [{theta: t, p: pnorm(t - icc_b), curve: "Normal CDF"}] : [])
])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 330, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: icc_norm, domain: ["This item", "Normal CDF"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: palette.rule}), Plot.ruleX([icc_b], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(icc_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{theta: icc_b, p: p2pl(icc_b, icc_b, icc_a)}], {x: "theta", y: "p", r: 5, fill: palette.main})
  ]
})
















Changing \(b\) slides the curve left and right without changing its shape: a harder item needs more ability for the same chance of success. The curve never reaches 0 or 1, so nobody is certain to get any item right or wrong. The slope slider is a preview: the Rasch model fixes it at 1 for every item, and relaxing that assumption gives the 2PL, which we take up in From the 1PL to the 4PL. (A challenge, especially if you know probit regression: turn on the normal CDF and find the slope that makes the two curves nearly identical. The answer is roughly 1.7: the scaling constant \(D\) that older IRT papers carry around so that logistic and normal-ogive parameters can be compared. Camilli (1994) traces where it came from.)


Code
quiz({
  q: "A person's ability equals an item's difficulty ($\\theta = b$). What is the probability they get the item right under the Rasch model?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.5", correct: true, why: "At $\\theta = b$ the exponent is 0, and $e^0/(1+e^0) = 1/2$. This is what 'difficulty' means on this scale."},
    {text: "It depends on the item's slope", correct: false, why: "Under the Rasch model every slope is 1. Even in the 2PL, the probability at $\\theta = b$ is still 0.5; the slope only changes how quickly the curve rises around that point."},
    {text: "1, because the person is at the item's level", correct: false, why: "The model never gives a probability of 1. At $\\theta = b$ the person is exactly as likely to get it right as wrong."}
  ]
})










The scale has no origin
Where is zero on this scale? Nowhere in particular. Add the same constant \(C\) to every ability and every difficulty: the model only ever sees \(\theta - b\), so no predicted response changes.

Try it: shift everything


Code
viewof shiftC = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "Add C to every θ and b"})









Code
shift_items = [{item: "Easy", b: -1}, {item: "Medium", b: 0.5}, {item: "Hard", b: 2}]
shift_people = [{person: "Ana", theta: -0.5}, {person: "Ben", theta: 1}]
Inputs.table(shift_people.flatMap(pp => shift_items.map(it => ({
  person: pp.person, "θ + C": (pp.theta + shiftC).toFixed(2),
  item: it.item, "b + C": (it.b + shiftC).toFixed(2),
  "P(correct)": p2pl(pp.theta + shiftC, it.b + shiftC).toFixed(3)
}))), {layout: "auto", rows: 7})























The probabilities in the last column do not move. The data can tell us how far apart people and items are, but not where zero is; we say the model is not identified without an extra constraint. Software picks one for you. mirt (Chalmers, 2012) fixes the mean of the ability distribution at 0, as the chess fit below shows. Programs that use conditional maximum likelihood (see the Go deeper callout below) instead fix one item’s difficulty at 0 or make the difficulties sum to 0 (Mair & Hatzinger, 2007). The choice is arbitrary, and results from two programs can differ by exactly such a shift. Remember that before you compare numbers across studies.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two analysts fit the Rasch model to the same data. One reports that item 7 has $b = 1.2$; the other reports $b = 0.9$. Which is most likely?",
  options: [
    {text: "One of them made an error", correct: false, why: "Not necessarily. If one program centers abilities and the other centers difficulties, every $b$ shifts by the same constant."},
    {text: "They used different identification constraints", correct: true, why: "If every item (and every person) differs by the same 0.3, the two solutions make identical predictions. Check the other items before worrying."},
    {text: "Item 7 is misfitting", correct: false, why: "Misfit wouldn't produce a clean shift in the difficulty estimate like this; a constant offset across items points to the choice of origin."}
  ]
})










People and items on one scale: the Wright map
Because \(\theta\) and \(b\) live on the same scale, we can plot them together. A Wright map puts the distribution of people on one side and the item difficulties on the other. It answers a practical question at a glance: is this test well matched to the people who took it?

Try it: build a Wright map


Code
predict({
  q: "Suppose the average person sits 1.5 logits *above* the average item. Roughly what proportion of items will a typical person get right?",
  choices: ["About 50%", "About 60%", "About 75%", "About 95%"],
  answer: "About 75%",
  reveal: "A gap of 1.5 logits puts a typical person at $e^{1.5}/(1+e^{1.5}) \\approx 0.82$ on an average item, and spreading people and items out pulls the average back toward 50%, to roughly three in four. Set the sliders below to check."
})









Code
viewof wm_mu = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean ability"})
viewof wm_bmean = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean item difficulty"})
viewof wm_bsd = Inputs.range([0.2, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Spread of item difficulties"})

























Code
wm_people = normalQuantiles(300, wm_mu, 1)
wm_items = normalQuantiles(20, wm_bmean, wm_bsd)
wm_pc = expectedPropCorrect(wm_items, wm_mu, 1)
wm_bins = grid(-5, 4.75, 40).map(lo => ({lo, hi: lo + 0.25, n: wm_people.filter(t => t >= lo && t < lo + 0.25).length}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 380, y: {label: "Logits", domain: [-5, 5]},
  x: {label: null, ticks: [], domain: [-45, 45]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX(wm_bins, {x1: d => -d.n, x2: 0, y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: palette.light, insetTop: 0.5}),
    Plot.dot(wm_items, {y: d => d, x: (d, i) => 6 + (i % 5) * 6, symbol: "diamond", fill: palette.contrast, r: 5}),
    Plot.ruleX([0]),
    Plot.text(["People"], {x: -22, y: 4.6, fontSize: 13}),
    Plot.text(["Items"], {x: 18, y: 4.6, fontSize: 13})
  ]
})







































Code
md`Expected proportion correct for this population: **${(100 * wm_pc).toFixed(0)}%**. ${
  wm_mu - wm_bmean > 1 ? "This test is easy for this group: many people sit above the hardest items, and we learn little about differences among them." :
  wm_bmean - wm_mu > 1 ? "This test is hard for this group: many people sit below the easiest items." :
  "Items and people overlap well, which is where a test measures most precisely."}`







Where people and items overlap, the test can tell people apart; where people sit far above or below every item, it cannot. That idea—precision depends on where you are on the scale—is the subject of Information, precision, and short forms.



What the model assumes
Two assumptions merit emphasis (Lord, 1980). First, the formula is right: in particular, a single \(\theta\) drives every response (the model is unidimensional). Second, responses are locally independent: once we know \(\theta\), knowing how someone answered item 3 tells us nothing more about item 4. Both can fail, and it is worth brainstorming how before we meet the formal checks. Two items that share a reading passage? A test where the last ten items measure something else? IRW vignettes look at how often each assumption holds across many IRW datasets: dimensionality and local dependence.


The sum score is sufficient
The Rasch model has a property that sets it apart from nearly every other item response model: the sum score \(r\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\) (Fisher, 1922). Once you know how many items someone got right, nothing else in their responses, not even which items, changes what we can learn about their ability.






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: in a logistic regression with an intercept, the derivative of the log likelihood with respect to the intercept is \(\sum_i (y_i - p_i)\), so at the maximum the model’s predicted number of successes equals the observed number.



For one respondent, \(\theta\) plays the part of that intercept. So the maximum-likelihood estimate of \(\theta\) is the value at which the expected number correct, \(\sum_i \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)\), equals the observed number correct, \(r\). Which items make up \(r\) never enters the equation.
That is easier to see than to state. Below are five items of increasing difficulty. Pick a response pattern and look at the likelihood for \(\theta\); then look at every other pattern with the same sum score.

Try it: sufficiency


Code
suf_b = [-1.5, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1.5]
suf_a2 = [0.5, 1.8, 1.0, 0.6, 2.0]
viewof suf_x = Inputs.checkbox(["Item 1 (b = −1.5)", "Item 2 (b = −0.5)", "Item 3 (b = 0)", "Item 4 (b = 0.5)", "Item 5 (b = 1.5)"],
  {label: "Correct on", value: ["Item 1 (b = −1.5)", "Item 3 (b = 0)"]})
viewof suf_model = Inputs.radio(["Rasch (all slopes 1)", "2PL (slopes differ)"], {value: "Rasch (all slopes 1)", label: "Model"})
































Code
suf_pattern = suf_b.map((_, i) => suf_x.some(s => s.startsWith(`Item ${i + 1} `)) ? 1 : 0)
suf_slopes = suf_model.startsWith("Rasch") ? null : suf_a2
suf_sum = suf_pattern.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0)
suf_same = patternsWithSum(5, suf_sum).map(x => ({pattern: x.join(""), mle: mle(x, suf_b, suf_slopes)}))
suf_curve = grid(-4, 4).map(t => ({theta: t, ll: Math.exp(loglik(t, suf_pattern, suf_b, suf_slopes))}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "Likelihood of this pattern"},
  marks: [Plot.line(suf_curve, {x: "theta", y: "ll", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          Plot.ruleX([mle(suf_pattern, suf_b, suf_slopes)].filter(Number.isFinite), {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})]
})














































Code
md`Your pattern is **${suf_pattern.join("")}** (sum score ${suf_sum}). The maximum-likelihood estimate of θ for every pattern with the same sum score:`









Code
Inputs.table(suf_same.map(d => ({pattern: d.pattern, "MLE of θ": Number.isFinite(d.mle) ? d.mle.toFixed(2) : (d.mle > 0 ? "+∞" : "−∞")})), {layout: "auto", rows: 11})







Under the Rasch model the column is constant. Switch to the 2PL and it no longer is: getting a highly discriminating item right now counts for more. The relationship between sum scores and Rasch abilities is one-to-one but not linear. On these five items the step from 3 to 4 correct moves the estimate from 0.50 to 1.67, and 5 of 5 has no finite estimate at all.
So which should you report, the sum score or \(\hat\theta\)? If the Rasch model fits and everyone took the same items, I’d report the sum score. It carries everything the model knows about the respondent, it orders people exactly as \(\hat\theta\) does, and nobody needs it explained. \(\hat\theta\) earns its keep when respondents take different items, as in Linking and equating: there the sum scores are no longer comparable and \(\theta\) is.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Under the Rasch model, two students both answer 3 of 5 items correctly. Student A got the three easiest items right; student B got the three hardest right. What do their ability estimates look like?",
  options: [
    {text: "B's estimate is higher, because B solved harder items", correct: false, why: "That is the intuition the 2PL (and a lot of common sense) would support, but the Rasch model says otherwise: the sum score is sufficient."},
    {text: "They are identical", correct: true, why: "The sum score is sufficient for θ under the Rasch model. B's pattern is less *likely* (it may suggest misfit), but the estimate is the same."},
    {text: "A's estimate is higher, because A's pattern is more consistent", correct: false, why: "Consistency affects how plausible the pattern is under the model—person fit—but not the ability estimate."}
  ]
})










Specific objectivity
The Rasch tradition has a name for the property it prizes: specific objectivity (Rasch, 1977). Comparisons between people should not depend on which items we happened to use, and comparisons between items should not depend on which people happened to take them. It is a demand we place on the data, not something the data grants us for free.
It is easiest to see through ICCs. If two items’ curves never cross, then everyone finds item A easier than item B, whatever their ability. If they cross, the ordering of the items depends on who you ask—and the statement “item A is easier than item B” stops meaning anything on its own.

Try it: do the curves cross?


Code
viewof so_bA = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Item A difficulty"})
viewof so_bB = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Item B difficulty"})
viewof so_aB = Inputs.range([0.3, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Item B slope (Rasch: 1)"})

























Code
so_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, so_bA, 1), item: "Item A"},
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, so_bB, so_aB), item: "Item B"}])
so_cross = Math.abs(so_aB - 1) < 1e-9 ? null : (so_aB * so_bB - so_bA) / (so_aB - 1)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.line(so_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "item", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          ...(so_cross !== null && Math.abs(so_cross) < 4 ? [Plot.ruleX([so_cross], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})] : [])]
})

























Code
md`${so_cross === null ? "With equal slopes the curves never cross: whoever you are, the ordering of the two items is the same." :
  Math.abs(so_cross) < 4 ? `The curves cross at θ ≈ ${so_cross.toFixed(2)}. Below that, one item is easier; above it, the other is. Which item is "harder" now depends on the person.` :
  "The slopes differ, so the curves cross somewhere—but outside the range plotted. Push the slope further from 1 to bring the crossing into view."}`







This is why advocates of the Rasch model hold to it so firmly: specific objectivity and sufficiency are what classical measurement in the physical sciences looks like (Wright, 1997). The catch is that the model has to fit. Consistency with the Rasch model comes from hard work—iterative item development and pruning of items that don’t behave—not from applying it to whatever data you have. Whether equal slopes are plausible for typical test data is an empirical question, and the 2PL discrimination vignette looks at it across many IRW datasets.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two items' ICCs cross at θ = 1. What does that imply?",
  options: [
    {text: "The items have different difficulties", correct: false, why: "Items with different difficulties and equal slopes never cross. Crossing requires different slopes."},
    {text: "The items have different slopes, so which item is easier depends on the person's ability", correct: true, why: "Below θ = 1 one item is easier; above it, the other is. That breaks specific objectivity."},
    {text: "The model has not converged", correct: false, why: "Crossing curves are a property of the fitted model (a 2PL or beyond), not a sign of estimation trouble."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: why the sum score is sufficient, and what follows





Assumptions: one respondent answers \(I\) dichotomous items; the Rasch model holds for every item; responses are locally independent given \(\theta\); the difficulties \(b_1, \dots, b_I\) are fixed. Write \(\varepsilon_i = e^{-b_i}\) (the item’s easiness) and \(r = \sum_i x_i\).
Factorize the likelihood. Using \(\Pr(x_i \mid \theta) = e^{x_i(\theta - b_i)}/(1 + e^{\theta - b_i})\) for \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\), \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{I} \frac{e^{x_i(\theta - b_i)}}{1 + e^{\theta - b_i}} = \frac{e^{r\theta} \; \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}}{\prod_i \big(1 + e^{\theta - b_i}\big)}.\] The data meet \(\theta\) in one place only, \(e^{r\theta}\). The product \(\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}\) depends on which items were right but not on \(\theta\), and the denominator depends on \(\theta\) but not on the data. Taking logs and differentiating gives \(r - \sum_i \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)\), the score equation from the main text.
Condition on \(r\). Add up the probabilities of all the patterns with the same sum score: \[\Pr(r \mid \theta) = \frac{e^{r\theta}\,\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)}{\prod_i \big(1 + e^{\theta - b_i}\big)}, \qquad \gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \sum_{\mathbf{y}:\, \sum_i y_i = r} \; \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{y_i},\] where \(\gamma_r\), the elementary symmetric function of order \(r\), is a sum over patterns and contains no \(\theta\). Divide: \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid r, \theta) = \frac{\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}}{\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)}.\] \(\theta\) has cancelled. Given \(r\), the pattern carries no further information about \(\theta\); that is the definition of a sufficient statistic. Three things follow.

Conditional maximum likelihood. Multiply \(\Pr(\mathbf{x}_j \mid r_j)\) over respondents and you have a likelihood for the difficulties with no \(\theta\) in it. Maximizing it is conditional maximum likelihood (CML). It needs no assumption about how \(\theta\) is distributed, and it gives consistent estimates of the \(b_i\) as the number of respondents grows (Andersen, 1970). Estimating every \(\theta_j\) jointly with the \(b_i\) does not, because the number of person parameters grows with the data (Neyman & Scott, 1948). The wirs analysis below uses \(\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid r)\) to compare the model with the data without estimating anyone’s \(\theta\).
Specific objectivity is a theorem. Take two items, \(i\) and \(k\), and condition on the respondent getting exactly one of them right. The same cancellation, with two items, gives \[\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid x_i + x_k = 1, \theta) = \frac{\varepsilon_i}{\varepsilon_i + \varepsilon_k} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{b_i - b_k}},\] which contains no \(\theta\). Whoever the respondents are, strong or weak, the comparison of the two items comes out the same. Swap the roles of people and items (two respondents, one item, exactly one of them right) and the comparison depends on \(\theta_j - \theta_l\) and not on \(b\). This is Rasch’s specific objectivity, derived rather than assumed. When the model fails, it fails in a checkable way: CML estimates of the difficulties from high and low scorers should agree, and Andersen (1973) turned that into a likelihood-ratio test. Problem 3 tries the two-item version on the chess data.
The converse. For dichotomous items, if some statistic is sufficient for \(\theta\) and is the same statistic whatever the item parameters, it is the sum score, and the model must be the Rasch model: logistic curves with equal slopes (Andersen, 1977). Fischer (1995) collects this and other derivations of the Rasch model. Under the 2PL, the weighted score \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) plays the part of \(r\), but its weights are item parameters, which is where From the 1PL to the 4PL picks up.







A note on estimation
Fitting the model is harder than it looks, because nothing on the right-hand side is known. The conventional approach, and the one mirt takes, estimates the item parameters first, integrating over the distribution of abilities with the EM algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981), and then estimates abilities treating those item parameters as known. Conditional maximum likelihood, from the Go deeper callout above, is the Rasch model’s own alternative. Estimating abilities and Estimating item parameters take these in turn.

Simulate
The code below simulates responses from the Rasch model, fits the model with mirt, and compares the estimated difficulties to the truth. It runs here in your browser; the first run takes about 20 seconds while R and mirt load.
Try changing np to 50, then to 2000, and watch the scatter around the line. Now change ni to 40: with 500 people the error barely moves (0.13), because each difficulty rests on the people who answered that item. More items sharpen the abilities instead, which is where Information, precision, and short forms picks up.

One detail trips up many first-time users: mirt writes the Rasch model as \(\Pr(x = 1) = 1/(1 + \exp(-(\theta + d)))\), so its parameter d is an easiness. Our difficulty is \(b = -d\), which is why the code negates it.

              length(pool_sd)))

  sd_theta <- sqrt(coef(m1, simplify = TRUE)$cov[1, 1])

The median table in the pool has a standard deviation of difficulties of 0.99; chess, at 1.75 on the pool’s scale, is more spread out than 74% of them. (The pool fixes the SD of ability at 1, while the Rasch model fixes the slopes at 1 and lets the SD of ability float, here to 1.22; dividing our 2.1 by 1.22 recovers the pool’s 1.75.) That spread is what you want from a test meant to separate novices from masters.
How do these difficulties relate to the simplest measure of item difficulty, the proportion of players who solve the problem?

Does the model fit? A common first look is the infit and outfit statistics (Wright & Masters, 1982): mean squared standardized residuals, which should be near 1 if the model is right. Values well below 1 mean an item is more predictable than the Rasch model expects (typically an item that discriminates better than average); values well above 1 mean it is noisier. How far from 1 is too far is the subject of Model fit and out-of-sample prediction.

For contrast, a table whose job is to show a setting where one ability and equal slopes describe the data less well: wirs, six items from the 1990 Workplace Industrial Relations Survey analysed by Bartholomew (1998). Each item asks whether a kind of consultation took place about the most recent introduction of new equipment (1 = yes), from informal discussion with individual workers (item 1) through joint consultative committees (item 3) to paid union officials (wording from the ltm documentation, Rizopoulos, 2006). Because the sum score is sufficient, the Rasch model says what proportion of respondents with each sum score should say yes to each item, without estimating anyone’s \(\theta\) (the Go deeper callout gives the formula).

Code

# Because the sum score r is sufficient, the Rasch model predicts the proportion
# endorsing item i among respondents with sum score r without reference to theta:
#   P(x_i = 1 | r) = eps_i * gamma_(r-1)(items other than i) / gamma_r(all items),
# with eps = exp(-b) and gamma_r the elementary symmetric functions (see the
# Go deeper callout in the lesson).
esf <- function(eps) {               # gamma_0, gamma_1, ..., gamma_n
  g <- 1
  for (e in eps) g <- c(g, 0) + c(0, g) * e
  g
}
p_given_r <- function(b, i) {        # P(x_i = 1 | r) for r = 0, ..., n
  eps <- exp(-b); g <- esf(eps); g_i <- esf(eps[-i]); r <- seq_along(b)
  c(0, eps[i] * g_i[r] / g[r + 1])
}
r_w <- factor(rowSums(resp_w), levels = 0:6)
tab <- data.frame(r = 0:6, n = as.vector(table(r_w)),
  item1_observed = as.vector(tapply(resp_w[, 1], r_w, mean)),

title: The Rasch model
text:
Problems

The logit. Show that \(\frac{e^x}{1+e^x} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\). Then show that under the Rasch model, \(\log\frac{\Pr(x=1)}{\Pr(x=0)} = \theta - b\). What does a one-unit increase in \(\theta\) do to the odds of a correct response, on any item?
Indeterminacy. Suppose \(\theta' = \theta + C\) and \(b' = b + C\). Show that \(\Pr(x = 1)\) is unchanged. Now suppose instead \(\theta' = k\theta\) and \(b' = kb\) for some \(k \ne 1\). Is the Rasch model still unchanged? What does your answer say about which feature of the scale the Rasch model does pin down, and how does it square with the difficulty pool’s chess SD of 1.75 against our 2.1?
Specific objectivity in the chess data. By the Go deeper callout, among players who solved exactly one of problems \(i\) and \(k\), the proportion who solved \(i\) should be \(1/(1 + e^{b_i - b_k})\) whatever their ability. Pick two problems of middling difficulty, take the players who solved exactly one, and split them at the median of their sum score on the other 38. Compare the two halves with each other and with the prediction. Repeat for a pair that includes Y15. What do you see?
Targeting. Draw the Wright map for chess_lnirt. For which players does this test give the least information, and why? Suggest the difficulty of two items you would add to the test to improve measurement for them.
Fit, two ways. Using itemfit(..., empirical.plot = i), compare several items in chess_lnirt and in wirs. Which dataset does the Rasch model describe better? Now run the simulation above with np = 2000 and ni = 50 and look at the same plots. What does “good fit” look like when you know the model is true?
Challenge: sufficiency in the data. In chess_lnirt, find two players with the same sum score but very different response patterns. Compare their estimated abilities (fscores). Then fit a 2PL (itemtype = "2PL") and compare again. Explain what you see. Then the open part: if the 2PL fits the chess data better, how much would you lose by reporting the sum score anyway, and how would you decide?

Going further

Rasch, G. (1960). Probabilistic models for some intelligence and attainment tests. Danish Institute for Educational Research; expanded edition, University of Chicago Press, 1980. https://openlibrary.org/works/OL4506215W. Where the model starts, including the case for separating people from items.
Andersen, E. B. (1970). Asymptotic properties of conditional maximum-likelihood estimators. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 32(2), 283–301. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1970.tb00842.x. Why conditioning on the sum score gives consistent difficulty estimates.
Andersen, E. B. (1977). Sufficient statistics and latent trait models. Psychometrika, 42(1), 69–81. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02293746. The converse: sufficiency of the sum score implies the Rasch model.
Fischer, G. H. (1995). Derivations of the Rasch model. In G. H. Fischer & I. W. Molenaar (Eds.), Rasch models: Foundations, recent developments, and applications (pp. 15–38). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-4230-7_2. The Go deeper callout, done properly and from several directions.
Rasch, G. (1977). On specific objectivity: An attempt at formalizing the request for generality and validity of scientific statements. Danish Yearbook of Philosophy, 14, 58–94. https://doi.org/10.1163/24689300-01401006. Rasch’s own statement of specific objectivity.
Wright, B. D. (1997). A history of social science measurement. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 16(4), 33–45. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3992.1997.tb00606.x. The case for the Rasch model, from one of its leading advocates.
Wright, B. D., & Masters, G. N. (1982). Rating scale analysis. MESA Press. https://www.rasch.org/rsa.htm. Infit and outfit, and Rasch analysis in practice.
Tutz, G. (2025). A short guide to item response theory models. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-87271-6. Chapter 2 is a compact modern treatment of the binary Rasch model.
Camilli, G. (1994). Origin of the scaling constant d = 1.7 in item response theory. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 19(3), 293–295. https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986019003293. The 1.7 in the ICC challenge.
Chalmers, R. P. (2012). mirt: A multidimensional item response theory package for the R environment. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(6). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i06. The package used throughout.
van der Maas, H. L. J., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2005). A psychometric analysis of chess expertise. American Journal of Psychology, 118(1), 29–60. https://doi.org/10.2307/30039042. The source of the chess data.
Bartholomew, D. J. (1998). Scaling unobservable constructs in social science. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C, 47(1), 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9876.00094. The source of the wirs data.

B., Kanopka, K., & Domingue, B. W. (2025). Realistic simulation of item difficulties. PsyArXiv. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jbhxy_v4). title: Factor analysis I: exploring dimensionality
text:
What this is for
How many things does a set of items measure? Classical test theory mostly assumes the answer is one, and a high alpha doesn’t check that assumption. Many instruments are built to measure several things at once: a personality inventory with five domains, a quality-of-life scale with physical and emotional subscales. And an instrument meant to measure one thing may not, as the reverse-worded items in the instrument-building lesson showed. Factor analysis is the family of tools for asking what, and how many, underlying dimensions account for the correlations among a set of items. It is one of the oldest ideas in psychometrics. Spearman (1904) proposed it to explain why children who did well in one school subject tended to do well in others, and it remains the workhorse for studying the internal structure of a scale.






Recall from From construct map to items: reverse-worded items guard against acquiescence, but they can cluster together by the direction they’re worded in, so a scale written for one construct can show two dimensions.



This lesson is about the exploratory version: we let the data suggest a structure. Factor analysis II takes up the confirmatory version, where we state a structure in advance and test it; it also asks whether a structure holds across groups, and shows that factor analysis and item response theory are closer relatives than they first appear.

Simulate
The code below builds a questionnaire with a known structure (by default, two correlated factors with five items each), runs parallel analysis, fits an oblique exploratory factor analysis, and prints the loadings for comparison with the truth. It uses the psych package (Revelle, 2026), with rotations from GPArotation (Bernaards & Jennrich, 2005), and estimates by minimum residuals (Harman & Jones, 1966). It runs in your browser; the first run takes a little while as psych loads.
Things to try: set loading to 0.4 or np to 100 and see whether parallel analysis still finds the right number of factors; set phi to 0.7 and ask whether two factors are still worth distinguishing; set n_factors to 3.

With the seed as written, the estimated factor correlation comes out at 0.18 against a true 0.3. That is sampling variability with 400 people, and a reminder that factor correlations are estimated with less precision than loadings. Download this code.

title: Factor analysis I: exploring dimensionality
text:
With real data
We use bfi2_zhang_2025, our main example: responses from 1,335 university students to the 60-item Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2; Soto & John, 2017), which measures five broad domains of personality with 12 items each. The data come from Zhang, Huang, Sun and Savalei (2025), who randomly assigned students to one of four response formats; we pool across formats here and return to that design in problem 4. Download the code.


Code
library(psych)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_2:v21_0.bfi2_zhang_2025/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(url)
wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
num <- as.integer(sub("self_BFI_", "", colnames(wide)))
resp <- as.data.frame(wide[, order(num)])
c(respondents = nrow(resp), items = ncol(resp))


respondents       items 
       1335          60 


Code
resp <- resp[complete.cases(resp), ]
nrow(resp)   # respondents who answered all 60 items


[1] 1199


A few responses are missing, scattered across items and respondents; we keep the 1,199 students who answered all 60.


Code
# The BFI-2 cycles through its five domains: item 1 is Extraversion, item 2
# Agreeableness, item 3 Conscientiousness, item 4 Negative Emotionality, item 5
# Open-Mindedness, item 6 Extraversion again, and so on (Soto & John, 2017).
domain <- c("Extraversion", "Agreeableness", "Conscientiousness",
            "Negative Emotionality", "Open-Mindedness")[(seq_len(60) - 1) %% 5 + 1]
table(domain)


domain
        Agreeableness     Conscientiousness          Extraversion Negative Emotionality 
                   12                    12                    12                    12 
      Open-Mindedness 
                   12 


Responses run from 1 to 5, and they arrive keyed: the BFI-2’s reverse-worded items have already been reversed, so a higher response always means more of the item’s domain (for Negative Emotionality, more negative emotion). Neither the table’s metadata nor its processing code says so, and the data can only suggest it. If the reverse-worded items were still raw, many pairs of items from the same domain would correlate negatively. The lowest of these correlations is essentially zero:


Code
# Are the reverse-worded items already reversed? If they weren't, many pairs of
# items from the same domain would correlate clearly negatively.
r <- cor(resp)
same <- outer(domain, domain, "==") & lower.tri(r)
round(range(r[same]), 3)   # Pearson correlations between items of the same domain


[1] -0.005  0.764








Recall from Classical test theory and reliability: the Mach IV arrives unkeyed, and there the data couldn’t tell us which items to reverse; we had to read them. Here the check is reassuring, but the published key (Soto & John, 2017) is what settles it.




The correlation matrix
Before fitting anything, look at the correlations with the items sorted by the domain they were written for.


Code
# Polychoric correlations treat each 1-5 response as a coarsened continuous one.
R <- polychoric(resp)$rho
by_domain <- order(domain)
image(1:60, 1:60, R[by_domain, rev(by_domain)], zlim = c(-1, 1), axes = FALSE,
      col = hcl.colors(41, "Blue-Red 3"), xlab = "Items, grouped by domain", ylab = "",
      main = "Polychoric correlations, BFI-2 items sorted by domain")
abline(v = seq(12.5, 48.5, 12), h = seq(12.5, 48.5, 12), col = "white", lwd = 2)









Code
off <- lower.tri(R)
round(c(within_domain = median(R[off & outer(domain, domain, "==")]),
        between_domains = median(R[off & outer(domain, domain, "!=")])), 2)


  within_domain between_domains 
           0.35            0.04 


Five blocks along the diagonal, and pale regions between them: the median correlation is 0.35 between two items of the same domain and 0.04 between items of different domains. The one band of blue belongs to Negative Emotionality (the fourth block, since the domains are sorted alphabetically), whose items correlate weakly and negatively with many of the others.


How many factors?


Code
predict({
  q: "The BFI-2 was designed around five domains, each with three facets. How many factors do you think parallel analysis will suggest for these 60 items?",
  choices: ["5", "9", "12", "15"],
  answer: "9",
  reveal: "Parallel analysis suggests 9, and the eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule suggests 12. With about 1,200 respondents, the data have enough power to pick up some of the finer facet structure within domains. Neither answer is 'wrong': how many factors depends on the level of detail you care about."
})









Code
set.seed(252)
pa <- fa.parallel(R, n.obs = nrow(resp), fa = "fa", n.iter = 20, plot = TRUE,
                  main = "Parallel analysis: BFI-2")









Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  9  and the number of components =  NA 


Code
ev <- eigen(R)$values
c(parallel = pa$nfact,
  kaiser = sum(ev > 1))           # the "eigenvalue greater than one" rule, for comparison


parallel   kaiser 
       9       12 


Code
round(ev[1] / ev[2], 2)           # ratio of the first to the second eigenvalue


[1] 1.7


Code
# The same parallel analysis on Pearson correlations, for comparison:
set.seed(252)
fa.parallel(r, n.obs = nrow(resp), fa = "fa", n.iter = 20, plot = FALSE)$nfact


Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  9  and the number of components =  NA 


[1] 9


Parallel analysis says 9, the Kaiser rule 12, against a design of five domains and 15 facets. Is that unusual? Across the IRW it is the norm. The IRW’s dimensionality vignette ran parallel analysis on 810 tables and found exactly one factor in only 3% of them; for the older 25-item Big Five Inventory in psychtools_bfi, built for five traits, it suggests six. Nor is it an artifact of the polychoric correlations, which Garrido, Abad and Ponsoda (2013) recommend for parallel analysis with ordinal items: on Pearson correlations the answer is 9 again. The formal criteria find more structure than the design names, because each domain is itself made of related facets.
The same vignette gives a baseline for how multidimensional the BFI-2 is. The ratio of the first to the second eigenvalue, 1.7 here, is a rough index of how far a scale is from a single dimension (larger means closer to one). The vignette’s 57 personality tables have a median ratio of 3.26, and the 25-item BFI’s is 1.91. The vignette’s tables have at most 40 items, so the comparison is rough, but by the IRW’s standard the BFI-2 is clearly multidimensional, as it was built to be.
The five-domain structure is still the one the instrument is built to score, so that is what we fit. The choice is ours; the data inform it but do not make it.


Five factors


Code
# Five factors, minimum-residual estimation, oblique (oblimin) rotation.
f5 <- fa(R, nfactors = 5, n.obs = nrow(resp), rotate = "oblimin", fm = "minres")
L <- unclass(f5$loadings)
top <- apply(abs(L), 1, which.max)
# Name each factor after the domain whose items load on it most often.
names_f <- tapply(domain, factor(top, levels = 1:5), function(d) names(which.max(table(d))))
short <- c(Extraversion = "E", Agreeableness = "A", Conscientiousness = "C",
           "Negative Emotionality" = "N", "Open-Mindedness" = "O")[names_f]
colnames(L) <- dimnames(f5$Phi)[[1]] <- dimnames(f5$Phi)[[2]] <- short
table(domain, factor = short[top])

domain                   A  C  E  N  O
  Agreeableness         12  0  0  0  0
  Conscientiousness      0 12  0  0  0
  Extraversion           0  0 12  0  0
  Negative Emotionality  0  0  0 12  0
  Open-Mindedness        0  0  0  0 12

round(c(median_main_loading = median(apply(abs(L), 1, max)),
        median_largest_other = median(apply(abs(L), 1, function(x) sort(x, TRUE)[2]))), 2)

                0.57                 0.16

N  1.00 -0.18 -0.22 0.02 -0.05

That is clean by the standard of the design: the median item’s loading on its own factor is 0.57, and its largest loading on any other factor is 0.16. The factor correlations sit fairly close to zero; the largest in size is −0.22, between Negative Emotionality and Conscientiousness (students higher in negative emotionality describe themselves as a little less organized and dependable).

Finally, the rotation point from above, on real data:


Code
# The same five factors with an orthogonal rotation: identical fit, different loadings.
f5v <- fa(R, nfactors = 5, n.obs = nrow(resp), rotate = "varimax", fm = "minres")
round(c(oblimin_rmsr = f5$rms, varimax_rmsr = f5v$rms), 4)

Identical root-mean-square residuals: the orthogonal and oblique solutions fit exactly as well, because they are the same model described in two frames. Rotation is a choice about how to read the factors, never about how well they fit.

text:
Problems

One factor. Show that under a one-factor model with standardized items and factor, \(\text{cor}(x_i, x_j) = \lambda_i\lambda_j\) for \(i \ne j\). Then show that, for any four items, \(\text{cor}(x_1,x_3)\,\text{cor}(x_2,x_4) = \text{cor}(x_1,x_4)\,\text{cor}(x_2,x_3)\). (These “tetrad” constraints were Spearman’s test for a single factor; Spearman & Holzinger, 1924.)
Reliability, revisited. In a one-factor model, what is the correlation between the sum of the items and the factor? Use your answer to explain why items with low loadings contribute little to reliability, and connect it to the proof that alpha is a lower bound in the reliability lesson. What does tau-equivalence mean in terms of loadings?
Planning a pilot. You are piloting a new 15-item scale written for three factors, and you expect loadings of about 0.5 and factor correlations of about 0.3. Using the simulation, find the smallest sample (to the nearest 50) at which parallel analysis finds three factors in at least 9 of 10 seeds. How does your answer change if the loadings are 0.4? What does this suggest about relying on one rule in a small pilot?
Formats. The BFI-2 data come from four randomly assigned response formats (itemcov_format: Likert L, Expanded E, and two item-specific versions, ISF and ISL). Fit the five-factor model separately in each format. Do the same items load on the same factors? Are the loadings noticeably stronger in any format? What would a difference tell you about the formats, and why does random assignment matter for that inference? (Zhang et al., 2025, is the place to compare notes; Factor analysis II gives the formal test of whether a structure holds across groups.)
A weak item. Find the three BFI-2 items with the lowest communalities in the five-factor solution. Look them up in Soto and John (2017), where the item wording is published. Would you drop them? What might they be measuring instead?
Challenge: PCA versus FA. Run principal() (PCA) and fa() with five components or factors on the BFI-2. Compare the loadings. Which are systematically larger, and why? Is there a number of items per domain at which the difference stops mattering?

title: Classical test theory and reliability
text:
What this is for
Every score contains error. A student who scores 27 on a test today might score 25 or 29 tomorrow for reasons that have nothing to do with what the test is meant to measure: a lucky guess, a misread question, a bad night’s sleep. Constructs and construct maps asked what a scale is meant to measure; this lesson asks how precisely it does so. Classical test theory (CTT) is the oldest and still the most widely used framework for thinking about that error. It is a theory of test scores, not of item responses: nothing in this lesson refers to the probability of answering any one item correctly. That is both its main convenience and its central limitation. The payoff is reliability, a single number that says how much of the variation in scores is signal.
Reliability estimates are everywhere. That doesn’t mean they are always meaningful, and part of this lesson is about when they are not.

title: Classical test theory and reliability
Classical test theory and reliability
text:
Core ideas

True scores and error
CTT grew out of Spearman’s attempt to correct correlations for the error in the measures being correlated (Spearman, 1904), and its standard statement is Lord and Novick’s (1968). The foundational idea is that a respondent’s observed score \(X\) is the sum of a true score \(T\) and an error \(E\): \[X = T + E.\] The true score is defined as the average score the respondent would get over (hypothetical) endless independent replications of the test; the error is whatever is left. From that definition, errors have mean zero and are uncorrelated with true scores, so the variance splits cleanly: \[\sigma^2_X = \sigma^2_T + \sigma^2_E.\] Reliability is the share of observed-score variance that is true-score variance: \[\rho_{XX'} = \frac{\sigma^2_T}{\sigma^2_X} = \frac{\sigma^2_T}{\sigma^2_T + \sigma^2_E}.\] It is also the squared correlation between observed and true scores (Lord & Novick, 1968). The trouble, of course, is that we never observe \(T\), so this definition cannot be computed from data. The rest of CTT is a set of tricks for getting around that.


The first trick: parallel forms
Suppose we have two forms of a test, \(X\) and \(X'\), that measure the same true score with the same error variance and independent errors. What can we say about the correlation between them? A little algebra (problem 1 asks you to do it) shows that \[\text{cor}(X, X') = \frac{\sigma^2_T}{\sigma^2_X} = \rho_{XX'}.\] The correlation between two observable things equals a quantity defined in terms of an unobservable one. Here is that fact in action.

Try it: parallel forms


Code
viewof pf_se = Inputs.range([0.1, 2.5], {value: 0.7, step: 0.05, label: "Error SD (true-score SD = 1)"})









Code
pf = {
  const r = rng(11), n = 400, T = [], X = [], X2 = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { const t = r.norm(); T.push(t); X.push(t + pf_se * r.norm()); X2.push(t + pf_se * r.norm()); }
  return {T, X, X2, pts: X.map((x, i) => ({x, x2: X2[i]}))};
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 460, height: 400, aspectRatio: 1,
  x: {label: "Score on form X", domain: [-6, 6]}, y: {label: "Score on form X′", domain: [-6, 6]},
  marks: [Plot.dot(pf.pts, {x: "x", y: "x2", r: 2.5, fill: palette.main, fillOpacity: 0.45}), Plot.linearRegressionY(pf.pts, {x: "x", y: "x2", stroke: palette.contrast})]
})


















Code
md`Reliability from the definition (true-score variance ÷ observed variance): **${(1 / (1 + pf_se ** 2)).toFixed(2)}**.
Correlation between the two forms in this sample of 400: **${cor(pf.X, pf.X2).toFixed(2)}**.
Standard error of measurement (the SD of the errors): **${pf_se.toFixed(2)}**, so a respondent's observed score typically lands within about ±${(2 * pf_se).toFixed(1)} of their true score.`







The two numbers at the top track each other as the slider moves, up to sampling error in 400 simulated respondents. The standard error of measurement in the last line is what reliability means for an individual. Reliability is a property of scores in a population; the standard error of measurement, \(\sigma_E = \sigma_X\sqrt{1 - \rho_{XX'}}\), is the typical distance between one respondent’s observed and true scores. A reliability of 0.8, between the two real scales below (0.70 and 0.90), still leaves each score with an error SD of \(\sqrt{1 - 0.8} \approx 0.45\) times the SD of the scores, nearly half their spread. Note, too, that CTT gives one standard error of measurement for everyone, whatever their score. We will see in Information, precision, and short forms that item response models let it vary.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two parallel forms of a reading test correlate 0.81 in a large sample. What is the reliability of *one* form?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.81", correct: true, why: "For parallel forms, the correlation between them *is* the reliability of each. No square or square root needed."},
    {text: "0.90, the square root of 0.81", correct: false, why: "0.90 is the correlation between observed and true scores, $\\sqrt{\\rho_{XX'}}$. Reliability itself is the correlation between parallel forms."},
    {text: "It can't be known without true scores", correct: false, why: "That is the point of the parallel-forms trick: two observable scores stand in for the unobservable true score."}
  ]
})










Alpha: reliability from one administration
Parallel forms are expensive, and test-retest designs have their own problems (respondents remember items, and they change between occasions). The appeal of Cronbach’s alpha (Cronbach, 1951) is that it gives a reliability estimate from a single administration, by treating the items themselves as a set of little parallel tests. For a test of \(k\) items with item variances \(\sigma^2_i\) and total-score variance \(\sigma^2_X\), \[\alpha = \frac{k}{k-1}\left(1 - \frac{\sum_i \sigma^2_i}{\sigma^2_X}\right).\] When items are scored 0/1, this is the same thing as the Kuder–Richardson formula 20, KR-20 (Kuder & Richardson, 1937); Guttman’s \(\lambda_3\) is alpha under another name (Guttman, 1945). The intuition: if items hang together, the total-score variance is much larger than the sum of the item variances, because the covariances between items add in; if they don’t, the two are similar and alpha is small.
Alpha rests on an assumption, though. Which one? Alpha equals reliability when every item measures the true score equally well (the items are “tau-equivalent”). When some items are better measures than others, which is to say nearly always, alpha is smaller than reliability (Novick & Lewis, 1967).

Try it: when does alpha equal reliability?
Six items, each an equally noisy measure of the same true score, but with loadings on it that you can pull apart.


Code
viewof al_spread = Inputs.range([0, 1.4], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "How unequal the items are"})
viewof al_err = Inputs.range([0.3, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Error SD per item"})


















Code
al_calc = (spread, err) => {
  const k = 6, lam = Array.from({length: k}, (_, i) => 1 + spread * (i - (k - 1) / 2) / ((k - 1) / 2));
  const S = lam.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0), varX = S * S + k * err * err;
  const sumVar = lam.reduce((u, l) => u + l * l + err * err, 0);
  return {lam, rel: S * S / varX, alpha: k / (k - 1) * (1 - sumVar / varX)};
}
al_now = al_calc(al_spread, al_err)
al_curve = grid(0, 1.4, 71).flatMap(s => { const c = al_calc(s, al_err); return [{s, v: c.rel, what: "Reliability"}, {s, v: c.alpha, what: "Alpha"}]; })
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "How unequal the items are"}, y: {label: null, domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Reliability", "Alpha"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.line(al_curve, {x: "s", y: "v", stroke: "what", strokeWidth: 2.5}), Plot.ruleX([al_spread], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})]
})
































Code
md`Item loadings: ${al_now.lam.map(l => l.toFixed(2)).join(", ")}. Reliability **${al_now.rel.toFixed(3)}**; alpha **${al_now.alpha.toFixed(3)}**${al_spread === 0 ? ", identical, because the items are equally good measures." : `, which understates reliability by ${(al_now.rel - al_now.alpha).toFixed(3)}.`}`







With the error SD at 1, the gap stays under 0.01 until “How unequal” passes about 0.5, where the loadings already run from 0.8 to 1.2. Against a reliability near 0.86, that is small, which is part of why alpha has survived. Push the loadings much further apart (at the far right one of them turns negative, an item pointing the wrong way) and the gap grows. But it only ever goes one way.






NoteProof: alpha is a lower bound on reliability





Assumptions: the classical model for each item, \(X_i = T_i + E_i\), with errors uncorrelated with each other and with every true score. The result is due to Novick and Lewis (1967); Guttman (1945) had shown it for \(\lambda_3\).
Write the total score as a sum of items, \(X = \sum_{i=1}^k X_i\). The test’s true score is \(T = \sum_i T_i\), and its reliability is \(\rho = \sigma^2_T / \sigma^2_X\).
Step 1: rewrite alpha in terms of true scores. Because errors are uncorrelated with everything else, \[\sigma^2_X = \sigma^2_T + \sum_i \sigma^2_{E_i} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sigma^2_{X_i} = \sigma^2_{T_i} + \sigma^2_{E_i}.\] Subtracting, the error variances cancel: \[\sigma^2_X - \sum_i \sigma^2_{X_i} = \sigma^2_T - \sum_i \sigma^2_{T_i}.\] So \[\alpha = \frac{k}{k-1}\cdot\frac{\sigma^2_X - \sum_i\sigma^2_{X_i}}{\sigma^2_X} = \frac{k}{k-1}\cdot\frac{\sigma^2_T - \sum_i\sigma^2_{T_i}}{\sigma^2_X}.\]
Step 2: compare with reliability. Both \(\alpha\) and \(\rho\) have \(\sigma^2_X\) in the denominator, so \(\alpha \le \rho\) exactly when \[\frac{k}{k-1}\left(\sigma^2_T - \sum_i\sigma^2_{T_i}\right) \le \sigma^2_T \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma^2_T \le k\sum_i \sigma^2_{T_i}.\]
Step 3: that inequality always holds. Writing \(\sigma_i\) for the standard deviation of \(T_i\), \[\sigma^2_T = \sum_i\sum_j \text{Cov}(T_i, T_j) \le \sum_i\sum_j \sigma_i\sigma_j = \Big(\sum_i \sigma_i\Big)^2 \le k\sum_i\sigma_i^2,\] where the first inequality uses \(|\text{Cov}(T_i,T_j)| \le \sigma_i\sigma_j\) and the second is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. Hence \(\alpha \le \rho\). \(\blacksquare\)
When is it exact? Both inequalities in step 3 are equalities only when every pair of item true scores is perfectly correlated and every \(\sigma_i\) is the same, that is, when the items’ true scores differ by at most a constant (\(T_i = T_j + c_{ij}\)). This is essential tau-equivalence, the case the widget shows at “How unequal = 0”. The proof leans on the errors being uncorrelated; if they are correlated (items that share a passage, say), alpha can overstate reliability, and the lower-bound guarantee is gone (Green & Hershberger, 2000).





Code
quiz({
  q: "A colleague reports alpha = 0.72 for a 12-item scale and concludes that 'at least 72% of the score variance is true-score variance.' When is that conclusion safe?",
  options: [
    {text: "Always: alpha is a lower bound", correct: false, why: "Only under the classical assumptions, in particular uncorrelated errors. Correlated errors (items sharing a stem, a passage, a method) can push alpha *above* reliability."},
    {text: "When the item errors are uncorrelated", correct: true, why: "That's the assumption the proof needs. Given it, alpha ≤ reliability, with equality only for (essentially) tau-equivalent items."},
    {text: "Only when the scale is unidimensional", correct: false, why: "Unidimensionality isn't what the proof uses. Alpha can be high for a multidimensional scale and is not a test of unidimensionality, a common misreading."}
  ]
})










Split halves and the Spearman–Brown formula
An older route to a single-administration estimate is to split the test into two halves, score each, and correlate them. The halves are only half as long as the test, though, and shorter tests are less reliable. The Spearman–Brown formula (Spearman, 1910; Brown, 1910) says how reliability changes when a test is lengthened (or shortened) by a factor \(m\) with comparable items: \[\rho_{m} = \frac{m\,\rho}{1 + (m-1)\rho}.\] Setting \(m = 2\) steps a half-test correlation up to full-test reliability. The same formula answers design questions: how long does a test need to be?

Try it: lengthening a test


Code
viewof sb_rho = Inputs.range([0.1, 0.95], {value: 0.6, step: 0.01, label: "Reliability of the current test"})
viewof sb_m = Inputs.range([0.25, 5], {value: 2, step: 0.25, label: "Length multiplier m"})


















Code
sb = (rho, m) => m * rho / (1 + (m - 1) * rho)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 280, x: {label: "Length multiplier m", domain: [0.25, 5]}, y: {label: "Reliability", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [Plot.line(grid(0.25, 5, 96).map(m => ({m, r: sb(sb_rho, m)})), {x: "m", y: "r", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          Plot.dot([{m: sb_m, r: sb(sb_rho, sb_m)}], {x: "m", y: "r", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast}), Plot.ruleY([sb_rho], {stroke: palette.rule})]
})


















Code
md`A test with reliability ${sb_rho.toFixed(2)}, made ${sb_m}× as long, would have reliability **${sb(sb_rho, sb_m).toFixed(2)}**. Notice the diminishing returns: each extra item buys less than the one before.`







Which split should you use? There are a great many ways to split a test in half, and they give different answers. Cronbach (1951) showed that alpha is the average split-half coefficient over all possible splits (for the Spearman–Brown version, strictly, when the halves have equal variances). We check this with real data below.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A 10-item scale has reliability 0.70. Roughly how many comparable items would it need to reach 0.85?",
  options: [
    {text: "About 24", correct: true, why: "Solve $0.85 = 0.70m/(1 + 0.70(m-1))$ for $m$: $m = \\frac{0.85 \\times 0.30}{0.70 \\times 0.15} \\approx 2.4$, so about 24 items."},
    {text: "About 15", correct: false, why: "That assumes reliability rises in proportion to length. Spearman–Brown has diminishing returns: 15 items give only about 0.78."},
    {text: "About 40", correct: false, why: "Forty items (m = 4) would give about 0.90, more than needed."}
  ]
})










Item analysis, and reading your items






Recall from Item response data and the IRW: IRW tables are long, one row per respondent–item response, so an item analysis starts by reshaping to one row per respondent; item means and sum scores are then column and row sums.



CTT also offers the simplest tools for looking at individual items. For each item we compute:

its mean (for 0/1 items, the proportion correct, often called the item’s p-value), a first indication of difficulty, where larger values mean easier items;
its item-rest correlation: the correlation between the item and the sum of the other items. This tells us whether the item is hanging together with the rest. An item with a correlation near zero, or negative, is either measuring something else or is keyed backwards.

That last point is subtler than it sounds. CTT assumes every item is coded so that a higher response means more of the construct. Many scales deliberately include items worded in the opposite direction, and those have to be reverse-keyed before any of this makes sense. How do we know which ones? We will see below that the data take us most of the way but not all of it, and that the last step is to read the items.

title: Classical test theory and reliability
text:
Simulate
Here is the lower-bound result from the proof above, on simulated data where we know the true scores. The code generates a six-item test from the classical model, then compares the true reliability, \(\text{cor}(X, T)^2\), with alpha. It is base R only, so it starts quickly.
Run it as is: with equal loadings the two numbers agree up to sampling error (0.865 and 0.86 with the seed as written). Then swap in the line of unequal loadings and run it again. True reliability rises a little, to 0.879, because the steeper items carry more signal, while alpha falls to 0.829: the gap opens, and in the direction the proof says. Change np to 100000 and the sampling noise goes away but the gap doesn’t.

With real data
We use two tables. The main example is gilbert_meta_1, the reading-comprehension outcome of a school-randomized trial of a literacy intervention for third graders (Gilbert, Kim & Miratrix, 2023; data at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/QARRYT): 30 items scored 0/1, where 1 is a correct answer. The contrast, for reverse keying, is the Mach IV, a 20-item attitude scale measuring Machiavellianism (Christie & Geis, 1970), in responses collected by Hunter, Gerbing and Boster (1982) and distributed with the lessR R package (Gerbing, 2026; IRW table lessR_Mach4). All code is base R; download it.


Code
# IRW tables are long (one row per response); reshape to one row per person.
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(colnames(wide))])
}
# Cronbach's alpha (KR-20 when items are 0/1).
alpha <- function(resp) {
  resp <- resp[complete.cases(resp), ]
  k <- ncol(resp)
  (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - sum(apply(resp, 2, var)) / var(rowSums(resp)))
}
# Correlation of each item with the sum of the *other* items.
item_rest <- function(resp) {
  tot <- rowSums(resp)
  sapply(names(resp), function(i) cor(resp[[i]], tot - resp[[i]], use = "complete.obs"))
}

What does a typical item look like here? The median item-rest correlation is 0.49, and 24 of the 30 items are at 0.40 or above. One is not: s_read_7_4 has an item-rest correlation of −0.01, essentially zero, although its proportion correct, 0.38, sits among the others in the plot. Whatever that item measures, the total score doesn’t share it. Since this test is the outcome in a randomized trial, that merits comment: an item that doesn’t covary with the rest adds noise to the total and so to the treatment-effect estimate. Problem 3 asks what alpha does without it.


Alpha, and all the split halves


Code
sprintf("%.3f", alpha(resp))


[1] "0.898"




Code
set.seed(252)
split_half <- function(resp) {
  k <- ncol(resp)
  h <- sample(k, k / 2)
  r <- cor(rowSums(resp[, h]), rowSums(resp[, -h]))
  c(raw = r, spearman_brown = 2 * r / (1 + r))
}
halves <- t(replicate(1000, split_half(resp)))
plot(density(halves[, "spearman_brown"]), lwd = 2, xlim = range(halves),
     main = "1,000 random split halves of gilbert_meta_1", xlab = "Reliability estimate")
lines(density(halves[, "raw"]), col = "#c2410c", lwd = 2)
abline(v = alpha(resp), lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Split-half correlation", "Spearman-Brown adjusted", "Alpha"),
       col = c("#c2410c", "black", "black"), lty = c(1, 1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")









Code
print(c(mean_adjusted = mean(halves[, "spearman_brown"]), alpha = alpha(resp),
        lowest = min(halves[, "spearman_brown"]), highest = max(halves[, "spearman_brown"]),
        share_below_alpha = mean(halves[, "spearman_brown"] < alpha(resp))), digits = 3)


    mean_adjusted             alpha            lowest           highest share_below_alpha 
            0.899             0.898             0.875             0.911             0.330 


The left-hand curve is the raw correlation between the two halves of each random split; the right-hand one steps each correlation up with Spearman–Brown. The adjusted estimates run from 0.875 to 0.911, and a third of them fall below alpha. But they average 0.899, against an alpha of 0.898 (the dashed line), as Cronbach’s result says; the last digit is the price of 1,000 random splits rather than all of them, and of halves whose variances aren’t quite equal. Any single split could have given a number a little above or below alpha.


Reverse keying: the Mach IV
The Mach IV is answered on a six-point scale, from 0 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Half its items are worded so that agreeing is the Machiavellian answer; for the other half, agreeing is the less Machiavellian answer. The IRW table stores the responses as given, unkeyed.


Code

  choices: ["About 0.70", "About 0.55", "About 0.35", "Below 0"],
  answer: "About 0.35",
  reveal: "Alpha is 0.37 unkeyed. Items pulling in opposite directions partly cancel in the total, so the covariances that alpha relies on shrink. It doesn't go all the way to zero or below: most item-rest correlations stay slightly positive, as the output shows."
})

Item-rest correlations can’t tell us which items are reversed, because the total we correlate against is itself a mix of the two directions. The published key reverses ten of them:

Could the data have found the key on their own? Automated keying, such as check.keys = TRUE in the psych package’s alpha() (Revelle, 2026), splits the items by the sign of their loading on the first principal component. Here is that split in base R:

mach_alt$m19 <- 5 - mach_alt$m19

             -0.05               0.05               0.71 


It recovers all ten published reversals, and adds m19. That is the one item the data can’t settle: its item-rest correlation is −0.05 keyed one way and 0.05 keyed the other, and the documentation that comes with the lessR data also lists it among the reversed items. Either way, it doesn’t covary with the rest of the scale. It is a reasonable question to ask respondents, but it is about something other than the other 19. I use automated keying as a prompt to read the items, not as a substitute for reading them: it got 19 of 20 items right here, and the 20th is exactly the one where a reader, not the data, has to decide.


Limitations worth remembering
Many of these were known to Cronbach himself. Alpha is a lower bound only under uncorrelated errors, and there are better lower bounds, such as the greatest lower bound or “glb” (Jackson & Agunwamba, 1977; Ten Berge & Sočan, 2004), and model-based alternatives such as McDonald’s omega (McDonald, 1999), which we meet in Factor analysis II. Alpha is not a measure of unidimensionality (Green, Lissitz & Mulaik, 1977). And reliability is a property of scores in a population: estimate it in a sample that is a poor proxy for the people you care about and the number may not mean much. For a clear example of that last point, see the IRW vignette on the reliability paradox in cognitive-control tasks, where tasks that produce robust experimental effects yield unreliable individual differences (Hedge, Powell & Sumner, 2018).
Finally, the limitation that motivates the rest of the course: CTT says nothing about individual item responses. It treats a test as a single score with a single error variance, the same for everyone. That is the assumption item response theory drops; Where CTT breaks shows what it costs.

title: Classical test theory and reliability
text:
Problems

Parallel forms. Suppose \(X = T + E\) and \(X' = T + E'\), where \(E\) and \(E'\) are uncorrelated with each other and with \(T\), and have equal variances. Show that \(\text{cor}(X, X') = \sigma^2_T/\sigma^2_X\). Where exactly did you use each assumption?
Attenuation. Let \(Y\) be a criterion (a gold-standard measure, say) with its own reliability \(\rho_{YY'}\). Show that \(\text{cor}(X, Y) = \text{cor}(T_X, T_Y)\sqrt{\rho_{XX'}\,\rho_{YY'}}\) (Spearman, 1904), and hence that a test’s correlation with anything is bounded by \(\sqrt{\rho_{XX'}}\). What does this imply for a new test whose validity is judged by its correlation with an established one? Loevinger (1954) describes the “attenuation paradox” this creates for test construction; read it after you’ve tried the problem.
The weak item. In gilbert_meta_1, drop s_read_7_4 and recompute alpha. By how much does it change? Now use Spearman–Brown to predict the reliability of a 29-item test from the 30-item alpha. Why do the two answers differ, and in which direction?
Split halves. In the split-half figure, about a third of the adjusted split-half estimates fall below alpha. Why is alpha not below all of them, given that alpha is a lower bound on reliability? (Hint: what is each split-half estimate a bound on, and what does it assume?) Challenge (open): is there anything about the splits that fall below alpha that suggests they are “bad” splits, halves that are not parallel?
Reading items. Look at the item-rest correlations for the keyed Mach IV. Choose the two weakest items and, from their content and the construct, argue whether each should be dropped, rewritten, or kept. For m19, does it matter which way it is keyed? Would your decisions change if the scale were used to screen job applicants rather than in research? Read Hunter, Gerbing and Boster (1982) alongside this problem.
Alpha at scale. Using the alpha() function from this lesson, compute alpha for five IRW tables of your choosing with 0/1 responses. Before you do, predict which will be highest. What features of a table (number of items, type of construct, sample) seem to go with high alpha? What would make you distrust a high value?

title: The likelihood and logistic regression
text:
What this is for
Almost every model in this course is fit the same way: write down the probability of the responses we saw, as a function of unknown parameters, and find the parameter values that make those responses most probable. That function is the likelihood, and it will be an object of keen interest from here on. It gives us estimates, it tells us how precise they are, and it lets us compare models. This lesson builds it up from coin flips, uses it to fit a logistic regression, and then points it at real item responses: 40 chess problems and the Elo ratings of the players who tried them. By the end, one small change to that logistic regression leaves us looking at the Rasch model.

Simulate
The code below simulates data from a logistic regression, traces the log likelihood over the slope, and finds the maximum two ways: with optim() on our own log-likelihood function, and with glm(). It’s base R, so it runs in a second or two.
Try n <- 50, then n <- 5000. How does the curve change, and what happens to the standard error? (With the seed as written, the standard error of the slope is about 0.43 at \(n = 50\), 0.10 at \(n = 500\) and 0.03 at \(n = 5000\): each tenfold increase in data cuts it by about \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3\).)

title: The likelihood and logistic regression
text:
With real data
We use chess_lnirt: 40 chess problems attempted by 256 players, from the Amsterdam Chess Test (van der Maas & Wagenmakers, 2005). Each player also has an Elo rating, the standard measure of playing strength from tournament results, stored in cov_elo and standardized to mean 0 and SD 1. Elo gives us something rare in item response data: an outside measure of each respondent’s skill. Download the code; it needs only base R.

Code
# cov_elo is the player's Elo rating, standardized (mean 0, SD 1 across players).
elo <- tapply(df$cov_elo, df$id, function(x) x[1])
round(c(mean = mean(elo), sd = sd(elo)), 2)


mean   sd

Does Elo predict success?
Start with the simplest model: one logistic regression for all 10,240 responses.


Code
# One logistic regression for all 10,240 responses: does Elo predict success?
m0 <- glm(resp ~ cov_elo, family = binomial, data = df)
round(summary(m0)$coefficients, 3)


            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)    -0.14      0.020    -7.1        0
cov_elo         0.50      0.021    23.3        0


It does, clearly. A player one SD above the mean in Elo has log odds of solving a problem 0.50 higher, so the odds are multiplied by \(e^{0.50} \approx 1.6\). The standard error, 0.021, is small because we have over ten thousand responses. The same slope falls out of the likelihood directly:


Code
# The same slope by brute force: the log likelihood as a function of b1, with the
# intercept held at its estimate, and the maximum found by optim().
loglik <- function(b, x, y) {
  p <- plogis(b[1] + b[2] * x)
  sum(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
}
b1_grid <- seq(-0.5, 1.5, length.out = 201)
ll <- sapply(b1_grid, function(b1) loglik(c(coef(m0)[1], b1), df$cov_elo, df$resp))
plot(b1_grid, ll, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#2780e3",
     xlab = "Candidate slope (beta1)", ylab = "Log likelihood")
abline(v = coef(m0)[2], lty = 2, col = "#999")









Code
opt <- optim(c(0, 0), function(b) -loglik(b, df$cov_elo, df$resp))
round(rbind(optim = opt$par, glm = coef(m0)), 3)


      (Intercept) cov_elo
optim       -0.14     0.5
glm         -0.14     0.5


The log likelihood peaks at the glm() estimate, and optim() on our own function lands in the same place.


Items differ
That pooled regression ignores something we know: some chess problems are far harder than others. What happens if each problem gets its own intercept?


Code
predict({
  q: "Every player attempted all 40 problems, so Elo is unrelated to which problem was asked. When we give each problem its own intercept, what happens to the Elo slope (0.50 pooled)?",
  choices: ["It gets smaller", "It stays about the same", "It gets larger"],
  answer: "It gets larger",
  reveal: "It rises to 0.83. This isn't confounding: Elo and problem are unrelated here. A logistic slope is a *conditional* effect, the effect for a given problem, and averaging easy and hard problems together flattens it. The average of many steep S-curves at different locations is a shallower S-curve. This is called non-collapsibility (Gail, Wieand & Piantadosi, 1984; Mood, 2010)."
})









Code
# Chess problems differ a lot in difficulty. Give each its own intercept.
m1 <- glm(resp ~ cov_elo + factor(item), family = binomial, data = df)
round(c(pooled = coef(m0)[["cov_elo"]], with_item_intercepts = coef(m1)[["cov_elo"]]), 2)


              pooled with_item_intercepts 
                0.50                 0.83 


The slope rises from 0.50 to 0.83. In a linear regression, adding a predictor that is unrelated to \(x\) leaves the slope on \(x\) alone; in a logistic regression it doesn’t. The pooled slope answers a different question, the effect of Elo averaged over problems, and it understates how steeply success rises with skill on any particular problem. My rule, for this reason: never pool item responses into one logistic regression without giving the items their own intercepts. The items are not interchangeable, and the model should say so.


Items differ in more than difficulty
Go one step further and fit a separate regression for each problem.


Code
# Finally, a separate logistic regression for each problem.
slopes <- sapply(split(df, df$item), function(d)
  coef(glm(resp ~ cov_elo, family = binomial, data = d))[["cov_elo"]])
slopes <- sort(slopes)
round(c(head(slopes, 3), tail(slopes, 3)), 2)


 Y15  Y31   Y3  Y30  Y26  Y29 
0.03 0.04 0.13 1.66 1.85 2.02 


Code
# Proportion of players solving the problems discussed in the text.
round(tapply(df$resp, df$item, mean)[c("Y31", "Y15", "Y29")], 2)


 Y31  Y15  Y29 
0.98 0.08 0.07 


Code
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(slopes, seq_along(slopes), pch = 19, col = "#2780e3", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Slope on Elo (logit per SD of Elo)", ylab = "")
axis(2, at = seq_along(slopes), labels = names(slopes), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.6)
abline(v = coef(m1)[["cov_elo"]], lty = 2, col = "#999")









Code
par(op)


The slopes run from essentially zero to about 2. Two of the flat ones are flat for different reasons. Y31 is the easiest problem in the test (98% of players solve it), and when nearly everyone succeeds there is little room for Elo to matter. Y15 is another matter. It is about as hard as Y29 (8% and 7% of players solve them), yet success on Y29 rises steeply with Elo and success on Y15 barely moves. Hold on to Y15: when we fit the Rasch model to these data in The Rasch model, it is the item that fits worst. Slopes that differ from item to item are the subject of From the 1PL to the 4PL.
Finally, a question to carry forward. Elo is an unusually good predictor, and most item response data come with nothing like it. What if we had no Elo at all, and instead gave each player an unknown parameter of their own, estimated from their responses alongside the problems’ intercepts? That is a logistic regression with nothing observed on the right-hand side, and it is the Rasch model.

title: The likelihood and logistic regression
text:
Problems

The derivative. Starting from \(\ell = \sum_i [y_i \log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)]\) with \(p_i = e^{\beta x_i}/(1+e^{\beta x_i})\) (no intercept), show that \(\partial \ell/\partial \beta = \sum_i (y_i - p_i) x_i\). Then use the simulation with true slopes of 0.5 and 2 and plot this derivative against candidate values of \(\beta\) for each. How does the shape of the derivative change as the true \(\beta\) grows, and what does that mean for how precisely \(\beta\) is estimated? (PS1#5)
A normal likelihood. Draw 100 values from a normal distribution with unknown mean and SD 1. Plot the likelihood for the mean over a grid of candidate values; then repeat with 10 and with 1,000 draws. Describe how the surface changes, measure its curvature at the peak, and compare \(1/\sqrt{\text{curvature}}\) with the usual standard error of a mean. (PS1#1)
Chess, your way. Using chess_lnirt, fit logistic regressions of resp on cov_elo with (a) no item terms, (b) item intercepts, and (c) item intercepts and item-specific slopes (resp ~ factor(item) * cov_elo). Compare the log likelihoods (logLik()). Which step improves the fit more, and is either worth its extra parameters? (PS1#2)
Two readings. A colleague looks at the pooled Elo slope and its standard error and says “there is a 95% chance the slope is between 0.46 and 0.54.” What would a frequentist say about that sentence? What would a Bayesian need to add before saying it?
No maximum. Construct a dataset of six observations for which the logistic regression MLE doesn’t exist, run glm() on it, and describe what R reports. Then change one observation so that the MLE exists. What is the item-response analogue of your first dataset?
Challenge: from Elo to the Rasch model. Fit glmer(resp ~ 0 + factor(item) + (1 | id), family = binomial) from the lme4 package to the chess data: item intercepts plus a random effect for each player instead of Elo. Correlate the estimated player effects (ranef()) with Elo. How close are they, and where do they disagree? What model have you fit?

Going further

Fisher, R. A. (1922). On the mathematical foundations of theoretical statistics. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, Series A, 222, 309–368. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1922.0009. Where maximum likelihood gets its name and its rationale.
Pawitan, Y. (2001). In all likelihood: Statistical modelling and inference using likelihood. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780198507659.001.0001. A patient book-length treatment of everything in this lesson, and a good deal more.
Mood, C. (2010). Logistic regression: Why we cannot do what we think we can do, and what we can do about it. European Sociological Review, 26(1), 67–82. https://doi.org/10.1093/esr/jcp006. The clearest account of why logistic slopes change when you add unrelated predictors.
Gail, M. H., Wieand, S., & Piantadosi, S. (1984). Biased estimates of treatment effect in randomized experiments with nonlinear regressions and omitted covariates. Biometrika, 71(3), 431–444. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/71.3.431. The same phenomenon in randomized trials.
Albert, A., & Anderson, J. A. (1984). On the existence of maximum likelihood estimates in logistic regression models. Biometrika, 71(1), 1–10. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/71.1.1. When the MLE doesn’t exist (problem 5).
van der Maas, H. L. J., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2005). A psychometric analysis of chess expertise. American Journal of Psychology, 118(1), 29–60. https://doi.org/10.2307/30039042. The Amsterdam Chess Test, and how it relates to Elo.
